newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African shares seen shrugging off fx relaxation.
newsitem.headline: S.African shares seen shrugging off fx relaxation.

text.p: South African shares are expected to shrug off the country's latest relaxation of exchange controls next week as a positive outlook for interest rates supports the market's recent record-breaking gains, portfolio managers said on Friday.
From July 1, South African individuals will for the first time be able to invest up to 200,000 rand offshore in a long-awaited part of South Africa's re-integration into the world economy.
But few market players expect any immediate flood of cash to go abroad. Instead they see a gradual outflow over the next few months.

"It will have an effect but it will be a longer term move. Maybe in the end we will see 6-8 billion rand in outflows, but it will be gradual," said Ryk de Klerk, senior portfolio manager at PSG Asset Management.
The South African Reserve Bank has predicted 3 to 5 billion rand of cash flowing out of the country.

Willi Jonker, executive director of portfolio management at Norwich Investments, said the central bank's prediction was probably going to be accurate, adding fears of a stampede out of the country were unjustified.
The Johannesburg Stock Exchange has been roaring all week, finishing at a third consecutive closing high on Thursday as the all-share index hit 7,402.7.
The market was spurred forward by the higher-than-expected May trade surplus of 1.75 billion rand and a lower-than-forecast May consumer inflation figure.
Both figures painted a rosier picture for possible interest rate cuts this year and provided market sentiment with vital positive support.
On Thursday a Reuters poll of economists showed a one-point cut in South African interest rates is possible towards the end of the third quarter and a certainty by the end of the year.
The interest rate cut speculation is in marked contrast to many major global financial markets and has sparked a surge in foreign buying of South African equity over the past month.
"We are in an environment where we will see interest rate cuts over the next 12 months, but elsewhere in Europe and the U.S. we will probably have a higher interest rates structure," de Klerk said.
This foreign interest is set to continue and many see it outweighing the outflows from the exchange controls liberalisation.
"Inflows are far stronger than the outflows," Jonker said.

However, while the underlying trend of the market is likely to continue upwards, next week may be buffeted by the second quarter close-out on Monday of local unit trusts. Some window dressing is possible as unit trust managers seek to ramp up some of their share prices.
This could lead to an unusually strong rise on Monday, followed by a dip in the rest of the week as more natural prices reassert themselves.
Some portfolio managers also see the market as needing a mini-correction after its recent gains.

"The market has been a little bit too hot this month and there may be a bit of a pullback. But I doubt whether it will be led by worries over outflows. It will be a natural and temporary correction," de Klerk said.
No major corporate announcements are expected next week but Tuesday will see the release of headline June gold and foreign exchange reserves with economists predicting a healthy rise.
